title: Participant Observation as an Anthropological Method
text:
The method that defines social anthropology is participant observation, and it is worth being precise about what it involves, because the phrase sounds almost like a contradiction. The researcher lives for an extended period, conventionally a year or more, in the community being studied, learns the language, joins in ordinary daily activities and keeps a systematic record of what happens.

Bronislaw Malinowski, writing in the nineteen-twenties after fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, set out the rationale. What people say they do, what they say they ought to do, and what they can be observed doing are three different things, and only long residence reveals the distance between them. A questionnaire collects the first two. Two distinctions organise the work. An emic account describes a practice in the categories the participants themselves use; an etic account describes it in the analyst's comparative terms. Both are needed, and confusing them causes trouble in either direction. Modern fieldwork adds reflexivity. The ethnographer is part of the situation and alters it, so a good account states who was asking, of whom, and within what limits. The result is deep rather than broad, which is a strength for understanding meaning and a real limitation when generalising.
points: Participant observation means living in a community for a year or more, learning the language and joining daily life while recording it.
Malinowski set out the rationale after fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands in the nineteen-twenties.
He argued that what people say they do, what they say they should do, and what they actually do are three different things.
An emic account uses the participants' own categories and an etic account uses the analyst's comparative terms.
Reflexivity requires the ethnographer to acknowledge that they change the situation they observe.
The method gives depth of meaning but is limited when generalising to other populations.
